speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision of the federal government to unpeg the Canadian dollar so that it can find its own level according to the pressures of supply and demand, has been diversely appreciated in political, financial and business circles.
In order to assess the government action, it is first of all necessary to analyze the consequences of the free exchange rate. I really said "government action", because after the fact, the only thing now to do is to imagine the consequences. I do not want to make the same inconsistencies of which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) accused the two previous opposition speakers, but I shall point to the honourable minister that it is impossible to set floating rates without expecting certain repercussions.
The minister should take care not to catch the disease of those he condemns.
Therefore, only after analysing the consequences of the government policy shall we know what steps the government should take to offset the adverse effects of a floating exchange rate, which means, in the present circumstances, a revalorization of the Canadian dollar, compared to other currencies, including mainly, the American dollar.
A rather simple way to understand the situation is to realize that at the closing of the stock exchanges or money markets last Friday, the American dollar in Montreal was worth $1.071%2>
whereas, yesterday, it was worth $1.03 only.
In other words, an American importer could, last week, import Canadian goods worth $1.07 while spending only $100 (U.S.), whereas, today, he can only import $103 worth of Canadian goods for the same $100 (U.S.).
Mr. Speaker, what I just said about the situation of the American importer also applies to other foreign importers. They will have to pay more to import Canadian prod-

DEBATES	June 2, 1970
ucts. Conversely, foreign exporters will be able to export more easily to Canada, unless the government indicates which steps it intends to take in order to prevent the Canadian industry and the workers from being adversely affected by this financial policy of the Canadian government.
The motion introduced by the Progressive Conservatives deals with the impelling duty upon the government to immediately announce a program designed to offset the increasing difficulties faced by Canadian exporters and primary producers, the difficulties faced by our domestic producers on the Canadian market, the undoubted resulting increase in unemployment; and a program that, by its immediate announcement, will ease the confusion among Canadians as to the financial and economic direction of the Canadian government.
We agree unreservedly with the terms of this motion, for it concerns the main aspects of the question and the main consequences of the revaluation of the Canadian dollar.
First, exporters and producers of basic products will have to face greater competition from outsiders on the domestic market and secondly, there will inevitably be an increase in unemployment.
On the Canadian stock market yesterday, shares in Canadian pulp and paper companies fell by 7.73 per cent, the greatest drop in at least five years. Why such a decrease in the price of those shares? Because the return on them will decrease as a result of lower sales abroad by pulp and paper companies.
As the exports will tend to go down, the companies' profits will be smaller and the dividends will decrease. But the pulp and paper mills and pulp and paper plants will not be the only ones to face the adverse effects of the government's financial and monetary policy.
One could read in the newspapers this morning that firms exporting basic products, such as nickel and copper, had shown yesterday great losses on the stock markets, while even the price of wheat had shown a drop of 6 cents per bushel in Winnipeg, as a result of the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. As for textile products, which are facing very close foreign competition, they will be doubly affected by the government's decision to free the Canadian exchange rate.
Only yesterday, Mr. Gerald Bruck, president of Bruck Mills Co., was saying and I quote:
The Canadian textile mills are the victims of imports that will have easier access to the Cana-
June 2. 1970	COMMONS
dian market while Canadian exports will be even more difficult, since Canadian textiles will cost more on foreign markets.
Therefore, it can be said that the government's decision will have a direct effect on several industries in the province of Quebec, especially in the Montreal, Quebec, Drum-mondville, Magog, Saint-Hyacinthe, Sherbrooke and Saint-Gregoire-de-Montmorency areas.
Canadian exporters and primary producers are penalized by the financial and monetary policy of the federal government.
Let us now deal with imports. We know that they will increase further as a result of the revaluation upwards of the Canadian dollar. Clothing, textile products, footwear and foodstuffs from the United States will be prejudicial to the Canadian fruit, potato and milk producers.
In the manufacturing industry, large stores will be anxious to buy radio and television sets, electronic equipment, and so on from the United States. This will bring about a slowing down of the Canadian production for domestic consumption to the benefit of foreign producers. We can foresee a decrease in exports and an increase in imports. This can only bring about a higher unemployment rate in Canada, the laying off of several thousands of Canadian workers who will join the ranks of the 700,000 already unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, If we agree with the terms of the Progressive- Conservative motion, it does not mean that we agree with the solutions they suggest. Indeed the Progressive Conservative party has none to offer.

At the time they were in office, they were faced with monetary problems. They then decided on the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. What compensation measure did they have to suggest? None. When they were in office, they did exactly the same thing the Liberals are doing now when they resort to monetary manoeuvers, for they had no other solution to off er.
What can we do now that the harm is done? What st-eps does the government intend to take? The Progressive Conservatives who have introduced the motion, are quite aware that the Liberals have no solution to offer in order to save the exporters from being penalized. They are quite aware that the Liberals have nothing to suggest to prevent foreign goods from flooding our markets and hurting our producers. They have put a tricky question to the government because they know

The increase in the rate of exchange fits well in the war against inflation. Imports increase, exports decrease and unemployment rises, thus easing the pressures exerted by the unions, with the long term and overall effect of bringing down the price levels which is the objective the government has in view.
We, of the Ralliement creditiste, agree that this objective is commendable provided producers, captains of industry and workers get a fair reward for their investments and their work. We agree that this objective is commendable provided consumers are able to buy the production offered, which is possible if prices are lowered to the level of the total consumer purchasing power.
For several years now, the Creditistes have offered a solution to that problem which neither the Conservatives nor the Liberals have been able to solve.
It is a matter of enabling the consumers to purchase, with whatever purchasing power they have, all the goods available. In other words, it is a matter of balancing the purchasing power with the prices.
We know that the real cost of production is consumption. For instance, if the annual Canadian production amounted to $80 billion and consumption to only $55 billion, Canadians who only consumed $55 billion worth of goods should be able to purchase that $80 billion production. They are the ones who produced it. It belongs to them. If they managed to produce $80 billion worth of goods while consuming only $55 billion worth, they should have the total production for $55 billion. Thus, it is a matter of lowering prices to $55 billion in order to enable Canadians to purchase the total production, the cost of which was set at $80 billion.
But where will that discount come from? If Canadians produced $80 billion worth of goods, they increased the real credit in Canada by that same amount in that year. But, if in the course of the same year, they received only $55 billion in salaries, benefits, dividends, etc, as purchasing power, financial credit must be increased by $25 billion if we want finance to reflect realities.
This is one of the solutions the government ought to apply to fight inflation, to prevent price increases and to allow the consumers to purchase the goods they produce.
For instance, why would the government not pay a discount to the Canadian producers

I should like to hear the minister's answer to these suggestions. When the minister will take the floor, we want him to say clearly what he intends to do to balance consumption and production. What assistance will he give to the consumers?
The Minister of Finance reminds me of a mariner who launches his rudderless ship on rough seas and waits to see what will happen.
This is not the way to run things. To govern is to plan ahead, and we hope that the Minister of Finance is more aware of the detrimental effects of the government's action. The Canadian population does not like a government that gropes its way.
Mr. Speaker, the people must be informed. Industrialists, dealers, farmers and all workers must know what will be the economic picture in the years ahead. That is why we are anxiously waiting for the minister's explanations.

I now wish to deal briefly with the reason why this policy has been introduced at this time. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) pointed out tonight, and as I elucidated in a question I asked yesterday, the fact was disclosed as recently as last Wednesday when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was asked by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) if the government was considering-not planning, but considering-the imposition of a floating exchange rate. The minister answered with a flat and immediate no.
As recently as last Wednesday the government was not even considering putting the country on a floating exchange rate. Suddenly, on Sunday afternoon the country was put on a floating exchange rate, a very drastic and far-reaching step. It makes one wonder why this was done and where the impetus came from. This is the way this unbusinesslike government does things.
Was it because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had pressure brought to bear, when he was in the Far East, by a great many low-wage countries? Was it suggested it would be a good idea to build a good feeling between Canada and our eastern friends by opening the Canadian market even wider than at the present time for imports from these low-wage countries? That seems to be about as logical an explanation as can be given. Otherwise, why suddenly out of the clear blue sky, without even considering this

proposal as recently as last Wednesday, was it suddenly introduced? It seems the Prime Minister got back, told the Minister of Finance what to do and he went ahead and did it.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
This new, floating rate of the Canadian dollar which seems to be settling down at around 96J cents U.S. is being imposed on the Canadian economy at a most critical time, a time when unemployment has reached its highest point in seven years and promises to rise still further. It is being imposed at a time when Canada is being flooded by low-cost imports from low-wage countries, causing people here to be laid off in large numbers in many industries and at a time when the government's restrictive policies are slowing down the economy and making it impossible for producers to carry out expansion plans which would permit the employment of more workers.
We are now confronted with a new dilemma which will cause great trouble for all producers in Canada. This new rate will have three main adverse effects. First, it will make imports into Canada cheaper in terms of the Canadian dollar and will thereby make them more competitive with Canadian goods. This will make it harder for Canadian producers to sell their goods in the Canadian market. Many orders which would normally go to Canadian producers will go to manufacturers abroad. This, in turn, will mean that fewer Canadian workers will be able to find jobs. Orders which would normally be theirs will be lost to foreign workers whose companies will receive those orders.
Second, the floating exchange rate will make it much more difficult for our manufacturers to obtain orders in the export market. Once again, because Canadian exports will be considerably more expensive, buyers in the export market will increasingly turn to cheaper products offered by our foreign competitors. Instead of a great many orders going to Canadian firms and being filled by Canadian workers, orders will go to foreign firms and employment will be lost to foreign workers in those companies.
Finally, the floating exchange rate will deal a severe blow to the tourist industry which as you know, Mr. Speaker, is our second largest industry. Not only will Americans and people from other countries find that it will cost them four to five per cent more to vacation in Canada, but Canadians who normally take their holidays in this country will find it is 22375-65

It is interesting to watch the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as he sits and smiles while I talk about what is going to happen. He does not care. To him, it could not matter less. He looks at this from a classroom point of view. These are facts and figures which involve people who will find themselves out of a job and hungry and miserable. They mean nothing to him. Read another textbook, write another chapter: who cares? That is the attitude of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
I think it is obvious to everyone in this chamber that if our industry is to remain competitive and retain its workers in employment, the companies concerned have no alternative but to reduce their prices by the same amount as the extent to which the price of the Canadian dollar has increased. This will not be easy because right now their prices are as low as possible. Industries producing for the export market, and the tourist industry, will need assistance from the Canadian government.
I believe this assistance should take two forms. The government should now reduce the taxes which industry pays to the federal government in the present fiscal year by an amount equal to the surplus which the minister declared the government had on hand when the last financial year ended on March 31 last, namely, approximately $350 million. I believe this surplus should be used immediately in this way, and that the new tax rates should be announced by the minister at the earliest moment. This lessening of the tax burden will help these companies to retain their position, bearing in mind that they will all be obliged to reduce their prices in order to remain competitive. Unless such steps are taken, a great many orders will be lost and very many Canadian workers will be laid off. There will be a tremendous increase in unemployment, something which we cannot allow at the present time because, heaven knows, unemployment is already serious enough.

As I was saying, the question of inflation and the government's policy on inflation is another debate entirely. What we are debating here is the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. This has a great bearing on U.S. inflation. The reason our dollar has been in high demand is this. Contrary to what the hon. gentleman who preceded me said, Canadian industry is not all that productive. According to DBS figures, Canadian production on a per man-hour basis is ninth in the world-not first, second or third.
The fact is that inflation in the United States has been due to a demand economy. The war in Southeast Asia, as the leader of the NDP said, has had a great bearing on U.S. inflation. The U.S. is also carrying on another war, the sort where it spends billions of dollars on the Apollo program. Except for the difference in intent, there is not very much difference between the two as far as the economy is concerned. It does not matter whether you produce trucks and vehicles to be blown up in Viet Nam or to be sent to the moon; the point is that the United States has rendered useless a great portion of its productive capacity. However, money has been paid in wages and there has been a demand for goods for disposal in the United States.
As a result of this inflation, our export program has prospered. We have had the value of all goods produced and we have been able to beat the prices of United States producers. This is why United States inflationary causes have had a bearing on the revaluation of our dollar. It has nothing to do with inflation in Canada, which is not a demand type of inflation at all.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) stated that we had
June 2, 1970	COMMONS
increased our exports up till now to about $800 million and the projection is that by the end of the year we will have a credit of about $2J billion. That is quite true. He also mentioned certain items of export such as gas, oil, steel ingots and so on. We are exporting these commodities, not necessarily because we are the best producers of them but rather because Canada is the only source of many of them. However, this paints the picture brighter for us.
The immediate result of the revaluation of the Canadian dollar is bound to be a demand for our industry to be more efficient. Indeed, this is essential. Despite all the gloom cast by the opposition, I still do not think we are heading into a depression. I think Canadian industry will be able to beat U.S. prices even though our dollar has been revalued upward.
I do not think the tourist industry will suffer very much, because nobody is going to convince me that the 5 per cent or 6 per cent differential will persuade Americans to stay home instead of enjoying the Canadian wilderness. It will have a slight effect, but we are not facing the doomsday suggested on the other side of the House. There will be a demand on exporters to become more efficient; but the rub comes when you ask where they are going to get the money with which to make their industry and their labour more productive. As long as we continue our restrictive policies, this will be impossible. However, I think the government will see the light and will soften its restrictions a little in order to allow Canadian industry to make itself more productive and to compete with United States production schedules and prices despite the increase in the value of our dollar.
Another factor that has not been mentioned is this. The Minister of Finance must remember that during the past five or six years Canadians have been borrowing a great deal of money from the United States, repayable in U.S. funds. There will now be a desire to take advantage of the upward movement in the Canadian dollar to repay this money in U.S. funds and then to borrow on the Canadian market. This is going to be difficult because there is already a shortage of money.
I should also like the Minister of Finance, when he gets a chance to reply, to explain how he intends to re-establish the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the U.S. dollar. Will this be done unilaterally or with the consent, advice and agreement of the United States? This question has not been answered.

We must therefore pinpoint the thrust of this debate to one issue: What alternative had the government at its disposal to combat the onslaught of world speculators? What would hon. gentlemen opposite have done? They condemn the government for freeing the dollar, but how would they have resisted the onslaught of speculators? With Mr. Rasminsky working in complete harmony with the minister of finance in fixing our monetary policy we had growth in monetary supply from 1963 to 1965. This government has foolishly attempted to curtail inflation by one quick, sharp slice of the knife. This is an impossibility. This has created high unemployment. Like it or lump it, we have to live with it.
We must remember that in setting the Canadian exchange rate free and having what is called a floating rate, we are dealing with a temporary situation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was forced into this action by an influx of foreign money into Canada. Let us analyse this. This influx

resulted basically from the unstable situation in the United States. It is unstable because of the growing unrest there, the Viet Nam position, the Cambodian crisis and the Kent University crisis. The Americans have slowly withdrawn their money from the United States stock market. In looking for another place to invest it, they decided on Canada. This is why we have had an influx of money into Canada. It has not necessarily been registered on the Toronto stock exchange. If we look at the Toronto stock exchange, we see that it has not dropped as far as the New York stock exchange. The reason is that it was bolstered to some extent by an influx of foreign money.
Not necessarily all foreign money enters Canada through the stock market. Foreign money enters Canada because of our high interest rate. We should not be proud of an influx of foreign money into this country when we are paying 12 per cent for first mortgage loans, 11 per cent or 12 per cent for guaranteed bank loans and 10 per cent or 11 per cent for standard bank loans. We should not be proud of the fact that money is entering this country when we are forced to exist with a deliberate high interest rate brought about by this government.
The Minister of Finance has said over television and in the press that this change could have been averted. He said we had one alternative. We could have injected a supply of money into the country which, in essence, would have created a situation where we would not have had to allow the exchange rate to float. There would have been enough money available to absorb the influx of foreign money. This is the step the minister should have taken.
In the city of Montreal, only 8 per cent of the sewage passes through any kind of a treatment plant. The rest goes into the St. Lawrence River. I should like my first remarks to be an indication of my support for the position outlined by the leader of our party in favour of the floating exchange rate. It is something we have advocated for a long time. I was somewhat surprised as I listened to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) making his speech in which he argued that the advantage of the fixed exchange rate was to protect the Canadian businessmen from the effects of fluctuation. However, I felt as though I had seen it all before somewhere, and I had-three years ago, written by the present Minister of Communications. I also listened with interest to the hon. members on my right. I wonder whether they realize what they are saying when they argue that a lower value should be placed on the Canadian dollar. I can just imagine those who are now on the government side sitting on this side of the House and saying the same things back in 1961 and 1962-saying the same things for the same reason: they were stupid government policies in both cases, high interest rates which encouraged the flow of money into Canada.

Those who see nothing but doom, gloom, disaster and worse in the freeing of the Canadian dollar from a fixed rate of exchange fail to understand the imperative need for flexibility in today's Canada and today's world. The rigid, dogmatic economic theories of the past are largely irrelevant. Economists ranging from Galbraith to those of other countries, including the Soviet Union, know that the imperative need today is for change. Modem government must be willing to introduce an economic mix and it must be willing to change that mix as conditions change. Governments unwilling to change in the light of economic necessity do not deserve to govern.
In light of the importance of exports to the well-being of Canada it must be obvious that a variety of compensatory activities and measures can be expected in the weeks and months to come. I join this debate, not to applaud the recent statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) nor even to criticize, but to ask what next will the minister propose. Certainly the decision to free the dollar on the international market and the lifting of the threat of credit curbs are only overtures to further changes soon to be made. Perhaps we can soon expect

What I criticize is the continual amateurish planning of this government, because certainly our Minister of Finance did not unpeg the Canadian dollar of his own volition. If we are to believe his March budget speech, he did not choose to abandon his plans to impose credit curbs. He was forced into both these actions to save face.
The minister knows full well that the move to set free the dollar is late. He knows the pressure began building up like a boil on the neck as early as December and continued throughout the first quarter of this year. What were the minister's advisers doing during this period when the Canadian dollar was straining at the upper limits of its pegged range? Certainly they were not doing very much advising.
Canada now has more than half a million workers unemployed. The freeing of the dollar will not help that situation in the short-term and may even aggravate it. Here I see the government walking a dangerous tightrope. Canada's export industries have been experiencing furious competition abroad and now Canadian products-I have in mind the primary products of the farm and the kind of products mentioned by the last speaker-will cost more. I am also keeping very much in mind that this policy will cause a delicate balancing act on the already rising unemployment scene.
If our salesmen in world markets are equal to the job, we may come through unharmed. They just might pull it off. But, Mr. Speaker, the minister has not told us everything, and the nation deserves to be told what his next moves will be. The western grain situation could not be worse. Already, before this announcement there was a drop in the price of export barley, wheat and other grains ranging to between 20 and 25 cents per bushel. We learned yesterday that the price of wheat has fallen by 6 cents a bushel. We are told that imports will be cheaper. Foreign tractors can be bought for less. Less what? Surely not money. The government can blame speculation for the need to free the dollar, if it wishes, but another fact which the government cannot deny is that it was forced into its move by that document written by and for the central Canadian businessmen on the Toronto-Mon-treal axis, the infamous white paper on taxation. In my opinion the white paper, by saying that only Canadian investment was a good thing, in the short-run repatriated much of our money, which created short-term pressure on the Canadian dollar. The government cannot deny that the white paper on taxation was a major factor in building up the pressure on the Canadian dollar at this time.
All this adds up to one basic truth, that the Minister of Finance and his advisers are incredibly poor forecasters. Now the Canadian dollar is free to seek its natural level. On the pure theory of economics, the currency of any nation should be free to find its real value. But pure theory is not realism and we realize that if the currency of all nations was floating there would be little stability left in the world. While Canadian exporters will find lower returns for their products and the domestic market will experience heavier competition from cheaper imports, I feel that freeing the dollar was unavoidable in the circumstances.
The government action does not even guarantee lower prices to the consumer. We have no assurance that the web of commerce involving the importer, the wholesaler and the retailer will allow the savings to be passed on to the consumer. Here again, there are too many uncertainties. There are too many nations like Canada which tie their economic future to the vacillations of international trade. This is why financial forecasting is such a hit-and-miss affair. I urge the government to consult other international agencies dealing with world liquidity and probe into techniques of allowing for change in the real value of a nation's currency without the constant fear of becoming the pawn of this perilous type of international gangster making his presence felt all too often, namely, the speculator in currency.
I do not think the freeing of the dollar will overprice it on the market for too long. There will perhaps be a brief flurry on the market, but I see it finally levelling at a slightly

higher value than it was. It will permit new freedom of action, if the government has any action. Certainly, some expansionary movement is now called for, but there we find ourselves blinded by the curtain of apparent inaction.
The reason the dollar should not go higher is that the government has already taken actions which will prevent large capital inflows. One is the white paper on the mining and oil industries in which reliable forecasts indicate that the oil exploration money coming into the country will be reduced by 50 per cent in the last half of this year. As a result of the white paper, mining too will be hard hit and will probably not attract so much incoming money. So far as our oil sales are concerned, we have had them curbed so we cannot expect a large outflow.
With regard to the wood products of B.C. and other parts of Canada, the housing starts in the U.S. would indicate there cannot be a large export of those products in the immediate future. Then we have the increasingly striking nationalism of some of our cabinet ministers who spoke about electronic barriers at the 49th parallel. All this does not help promote confidence or the freedom of action of money coming into Canada.
What Canada needs now is the introduction of full employment policies to counter the threat of heavy foreign competition. We must have no more talk of the white paper's threats to the primary industries. Our western wheat is becoming more expensive because of this freeing of the dollar, and so more difficult to sell. We need some help in that area. The minister claimed on Sunday that some adjustment will be made to help the farmer. What adjustment, we ask. An announcement of aid for falling grain prices should have been made at the same time. Let the government make the adjustment quickly. It should not falter any further because quick and decisive action is imperative.
This may be the government's last chance in its battle with inflation. If it misreads the economy this time, we may well be in for a disastrous recession. We on this side of the House do not want to see that happen even though another party sits on the treasury benches. Should the economists who have the minister's ear begin to call the play more correctly, I feel there is a chance now to tie down the dangerous inflationary spiral. Then we will all applaud.

In addition, foreign borrowing by our municipalities and provinces has been carrying on at a high level. Canadian investors have been continuing to show their confidence in Canada by buying these securities and investing in this country. This is contrary to what the opposition has been saying for several months. I pointed out to the opposition that they were wrong when they said that all the money was moving out of Canada because of the white paper. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is quite unrealistic. We had no way of knowing with any precision the extent of the appreciation which would take place. We all know that our exporters had real difficulties when the Canadian dollar was overvalued, but they have now had a long period of stability and of consolidation, in which they have been able to stake out their position in export markets.
